RSSY: Two strategies stacked in one fund: full exposure to large US stocks, plus an equal second layer of futures across bonds, commodities and currencies run for yield. The stacking lets every dollar work twice, aiming for stock growth alongside a futures income stream that does not depend on the market's direction.
ACEP: US companies picked by active managers as a core portfolio, with technology about a third but unusually large slices of energy, miners and banks alongside. It is a stock picker's blend fund, so its sector mix and results can wander well away from a standard index fund.
LFGY: A basket of crypto and technology companies, bitcoin miners, payment firms and chipmakers, with call options sold against the holdings to generate income. It turns a volatile corner of the market into a payout stream, giving up some upside when crypto stocks surge.
BCLO: The middle and lower layers of CLOs, bundles of business loans rated from BBB down to B, actively picked for their higher interest payments. Those layers pay more than top-rated CLOs because they absorb loan losses sooner, making this an income fund with real credit risk.
XSEP: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, with an enhanced payoff design and a cushion that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each September. It trades a cap on gains for partial protection plus a boost to modest returns.
INEQ: Dividend-paying companies outside the US, led by banks at about a third, with oil, mining and industrial firms adding more income weight. It is built as an international income holding, favoring established payers in Europe, Asia and beyond over fast growers.
EDGU: A dynamically managed mix of US stock funds, currently heavy in technology and big growth names with a slice of small value companies. Managers shift sector and size exposures as their outlook changes, so the fund is a tactical core holding rather than a fixed index mix.
JHHY: High yield corporate bonds chosen by active managers, lending in US dollars to companies rated below investment grade across many industries. It is built for income, and active selection is meant to dodge the weakest borrowers, though defaults and price drops remain part of junk bond investing.
BMVP: Fifty US stocks chosen by a combined score for momentum, low volatility, cheap valuation and profitability, picked sector by sector so no industry dominates. It is a balanced multifactor approach: instead of betting on one investing style, it blends four in roughly equal measure.
DDFO: Built to gain from moves in either direction over its one-year October period: it can profit when large US stocks fall moderately as well as when they rise, up to a cap. The 15 in its name is the buffer meant to absorb deeper losses first.
BLDX: Infrastructure companies worldwide chosen with a sustainability lens: clean power utilities, water systems, railroads, data centers and materials for building. It is a defensive stock holding with a green filter, favoring businesses that conserve resources or widen access to essentials like water, energy and data.
HYSA: A fund built from three high yield bond funds sliced by credit rating, the stronger BB names, then B, then a small piece of risky CCC debt. Blending the slices gives broad junk bond income in one holding, with the mix actively adjusted as credit conditions change.
HAWG: Large US stocks, heavy in technology at about half the fund, paired with a hedging system that can pull back when its trend signals turn negative. It aims to stay invested for growth in good times and step aside in bad ones, though the hedge can also mute recoveries.
AGGA: An actively allocated bundle of bond funds covering corporate debt, Treasuries of different maturities, high yield bonds and top-rated loan bundles. Managers move the mix as rates and credit shift, making it a flexible core bond holding rather than a fixed slice of the bond market.
NBFC: Credit of almost every kind, corporate bonds, bundled loans, mortgage debt and other securitized borrowing, chosen flexibly by active managers hunting income. It can roam wherever lending looks attractive, which means credit quality and risk vary as the managers trade safety for yield.
ACES: Clean energy companies in the US and Canada: solar panel and inverter makers, wind and geothermal power producers, hydrogen firms and electric vehicle names. It is a focused bet on the energy transition, so it swings with policy support and green energy sentiment.
AFK: Companies across Africa, from South African and Moroccan banks to gold and copper miners and telecom firms, with materials and financials each about a third. It is one of the few single-continent bets available, tied to African growth, commodity prices and often fragile currencies.
AJUL: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to protect against losses over a two-year outcome period that ends in July. In exchange for that defined protection it gives up gains beyond a preset cap, and the longer two-year window sets it apart from yearly versions.
WTBN: A hand-picked set of five to twenty bond funds chosen by Bianco Research, spanning Treasuries of many maturities, corporate bonds and inflation-protected debt. The research-driven selection sets it apart from plain core bond funds, aiming for total return by shifting the mix as the outlook changes.
CLSM: A rotating handful of US sector funds, currently concentrated in technology, big growth stocks and consumer staples, plus a little gold. It chases whichever sectors are leading while keeping a moderate stance, so the lineup can change completely as market leadership rotates.
MAGY: The Magnificent Seven, the small group of giant technology stocks that dominate the modern market, with call options sold against them every week for income. Weekly option premiums are the point, so it pays out steadily while giving up part of the gains when those stocks jump.
DALI: A rotation among First Trust stock funds guided by relative strength, favoring whichever styles and sectors have been performing best recently. The lineup shifts as trends change, currently leaning industrial, making it a momentum strategy that can look very different from one season to the next.
GXRP: A single cryptocurrency, XRP, held directly rather than through futures, giving brokerage-account exposure to the coin's price. Grayscale's trust format sets it apart from newer rivals, and like all single-coin funds it can swing violently with the crypto market's mood.
HISF: A blend of First Trust bond funds chosen to maximize income, mixing corporate debt, loans and other higher-yielding corners of the bond market. It is a fund of funds built purely for payout, so credit quality runs lower and price swings run larger than in core bond funds.
MGOV: Intermediate-term US government debt: Treasuries plus agency mortgage bonds issued by Fannie Mae and similar bodies, actively managed. Because the borrowers are the government and its agencies, credit risk is minimal, and the fund is built for steady income with moderate sensitivity to interest rates.
HYDR: Companies building the hydrogen economy: fuel cell makers, hydrogen producers and the industrial firms supplying them, mostly small and mid-sized names worldwide. Two holdings alone are nearly a third of the fund, so it is a concentrated bet on a young technology that still loses money widely.
INTM: Municipal bonds maturing in the intermediate range, from states, cities, schools and utilities across the US, actively managed for tax-exempt income. The interest escapes federal income tax, which sets it apart from taxable bond funds and suits investors in higher tax brackets.
EAPR: Options on emerging market stocks, from Asian technology firms to banks and retailers across the developing world, arranged to absorb a first slice of losses over a one-year period that resets each April. It softens the famously rough ride of emerging markets, at the cost of capped gains.
NVBW: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to absorb the first 20 percent of losses over a one-year period running from November to October. In exchange for that deep buffer it accepts a cap on gains, suiting investors who fear a serious downturn most.
PAB: The broad US investment grade bond market, Treasuries, government mortgage bonds and corporate debt, actively managed rather than indexed. Managers adjust maturities and credit as they see value, making it a flexible core bond holding whose results depend on those calls as much as on rates.
XDIV: Large US stocks across every major industry, managed with a twist: it is designed to avoid collecting dividend payouts, shifting holdings around payment dates. That suits investors in taxable accounts who prefer no dividend income, though the maneuvering can make it trail a plain index fund slightly.
FFND: Growth companies around the world picked by active managers, at least 30 percent of them outside the US, with technology about a third of the fund. It is one global growth portfolio rather than separate US and foreign funds, so stock selection drives everything.
EMCB: Corporate bonds from companies in developing countries, issued in US dollars by miners, banks, bottlers and telecom firms across Latin America, Asia and beyond. It pays more than developed-market corporate debt in exchange for emerging market risk, and dollar denomination removes direct currency swings.
JUNP: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, with a buffer against a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each June (the 12 in its name). It trades gains past a cap for that protection, aiming for a calmer version of stock market exposure.
FCVT: Convertible securities, bonds and preferred shares that can turn into stock, issued mostly by technology and growth companies. Convertibles behave like a hybrid: they pay interest and fall less than stocks in downturns, but join in part of the rise when the underlying shares climb.
NCLD: Neocloud companies, the new breed of cloud firms renting out powerful graphics chips for artificial intelligence training, many of them converted bitcoin miners. It is a narrow, young and concentrated bet on AI computing demand, so sharp swings are part of the package.
GMOV: Large US companies that GMO's managers judge underpriced, spread across banks, drugmakers, technology and energy with an eye on quality as well as cheapness. It is an active value fund from a firm known for valuation discipline, so it often shuns whatever the market currently loves.
IMVP: Large and mid-sized Indian companies screened on four factors at once: momentum, value, low volatility and profitability. The factor scoring sets it apart from plain India index funds, aiming for a steadier mix of Indian growth across banks, software, consumer and energy names.
ITDF: A retirement fund aimed at people planning to retire around 2050, currently holding mostly stock funds from around the world with a small slice of bonds. Its mix automatically grows more cautious as 2050 approaches, shifting from growth toward income and capital preservation over time.
AVNC: Companies across developed and emerging markets outside the US, mixing direct stock holdings with broad international funds, tilted toward cheaper and more profitable firms. Avantis builds it as a core international holding, so the value tilt and wide diversification set it apart from plain index funds.
EXUS: A focused portfolio of large companies outside the US, from Asian chipmakers to European banks, aerospace and industrial firms, with technology about a third. Nomura's managers pick a select group rather than the whole market, making it an active core international holding with concentrated convictions.
JPMB: Bonds sold by governments of developing countries, Brazil, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Colombia and others, all issued in US dollars. It pays higher interest than rich-country government debt in exchange for the risk that a borrowing government struggles, and dollar issuance removes local currency swings.
DDFD: Built to gain from moves in either direction over its one-year December period: it can profit when large US stocks fall moderately as well as when they rise, up to a cap. The 15 in its name is the buffer meant to absorb deeper losses first.
FITZ: Companies chosen as must-haves for the decades ahead, businesses positioned to benefit from long-running structural changes in technology, health and industry. It is an actively managed growth portfolio built around themes rather than sectors, so its results hinge on those long-term calls being right.
PIFI: Intermediate US bonds, mostly Treasuries and government agency debt, actively managed with maturities kept between zero and ten years. It is a quality-first core bond holding, and active management of its maturity mix is meant to soften the blow when interest rates rise.
JHCB: Bonds issued by big US companies, banks, tech firms, utilities and drugmakers, all investment grade, with room for some bank loans alongside. It is a straightforward corporate income holding, paying more than government bonds in exchange for lending to companies rather than the Treasury.
PSMD: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged under a structured outcome design that cushions a middle range of losses over a period resetting each January. It trades some upside for that moderate protection, aiming for a calmer ride than owning stocks outright.
OASC: Small and mid-sized US companies spread across finance, technology, health care and consumer firms, actively enhanced beyond a plain index approach. Smaller companies offer more growth potential and more volatility, and this fund's active selection aims to tilt those odds in the investor's favor.
EVX: Companies that clean up: garbage collection giants, water treatment and drainage firms, recycling and environmental consultants, mostly industrial names. It is a focused bet on the unglamorous business of waste and water, which tends to grow steadily regardless of economic fashion.
BITA: Bitcoin exposure paired with covered call options sold against it each month, turning the cryptocurrency's price swings into premium income. The calls cap gains when bitcoin jumps, so it is an income-first way to hold crypto, with payouts that vary as volatility changes.
